2026_000_specialeducation_board_narrativ.paragraph: A board narrative summary dated June 2026 presents the Troy School District's proposed special education budget reductions, developed through a structured scoring process in which each proposal was evaluated across six weighted criteria — impact on student learning, equity, legal and compliance risk, cost savings, feasibility, and stakeholder support — and then sorted into tiers. Eight proposals, four in classroom instruction and four in non-instructional support, carry $3,229,885 in combined annual savings. The stated rationale is cost growth outpacing enrollment: special education costs rose 74%, from $16,744,610 in 2018–2019 to $29,210,999 in 2024–2025, an increase of $12,466,389, while the number of students served moved from 1,332 to 1,367.
2026_000_specialeducation_board_narrativ.page:
**Document**
Board Narrative Summary — Special Education Budget Reductions, Proposed Reduction Scenario, June 2026, Troy School District.

**Method**
Each proposal was evaluated across six weighted criteria: impact on student learning, equity, legal and compliance risk, cost savings, feasibility, and stakeholder support. Weighted scores placed each proposal into a tier. Tier 1 = strong candidate (4.0–5.0); Tier 2 = consider (3.0–3.9); Tier 3 = high risk, requires further study (below 3.0). Savings figures reflect actual FTE and actual dollar savings as entered in the scoring matrix.

**Why special education is in the reduction scenario**
Costs grew far faster than the population served over the six-year window cited.

| Description | 2018–2019 | 2024–2025 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Special Education Costs – IEP & non-IEP | $16,744,610 | $29,210,999 | +$12,466,389 (74%) |
| Special Education Student Count | 1,332 | 1,367 | +35 (3%) |

The summary also cites a state-led shift in how certain special education services are delivered; several proposals align district staffing to new county-level service plans and county targets.

**Category summary**

| Category | # of Proposals | Annual Savings | Tier Mix (T1/T2/T3) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Special Education – Classroom Instruction | 4 | $1,396,573 | 2 / 1 / 1 |
| Special Education – Non-Instructional | 4 | $1,833,312 | 2 / 2 / 0 |
| Total Special Education Reductions | 8 | $3,229,885 | 4 / 3 / 1 |

**Classroom instruction reductions — $1,396,573**

| Proposal | Annual Savings | Score | Tier | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Adjust TC/RR staff to meet county targets (3.7 Elementary, 3.6 Secondary) | $635,100 | 2.95 | Tier 3 | Flag for review |
| Teacher reduction based on new county level plan (3 L4, 1 ECP) | $348,000 | 4.10 | Tier 1 | Recommended |
| Paraprofessional reduction based on new county level plan | $236,270 | 4.10 | Tier 1 | Recommended |
| Elementary Resource Room paraprofessionals reduction | $177,203 | 3.85 | Tier 2 | Consider |
| Subtotal | $1,396,573 | | | |

The Teacher Consultant / Resource Room (TC/RR) adjustment is the only Tier 3 proposal in the special education set and, per the scoring framework, warrants further study before adoption.

**Non-instructional reductions — $1,833,312**

| Proposal | Annual Savings | Score | Tier | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Student Support Aide – Gen Ed (from 158 to 104 FTE) | $1,334,362 | 4.15 | Tier 1 | Recommended |
| Social Workers reduction (from 24.4 to 21.4 FTE) | $348,000 | 3.90 | Tier 2 | Consider |
| Psychologist reduction (from 10 to 9 FTE) | $116,000 | 3.90 | Tier 2 | Consider |
| Special Education Secretary | $34,951 | 4.35 | Tier 1 | Recommended |
| Subtotal | $1,833,312 | | | |

The Student Support Aide reduction is described as the largest single special education reduction in the entire scenario, accounting for more than $1.3 million in savings. Social worker and psychologist reductions are noted as candidates for phased implementation.

**Risk and planning**
Of the eight proposals, four are Tier 1 (recommended), three are Tier 2 (consider, with additional planning), and one is Tier 3 (high risk). The four Tier 1 proposals are described as totaling roughly $1.95 million and are recommended for inclusion. Proposals scoring below 4.0 may still be included if savings are critical to meeting the reduction goal, but require additional planning, communication, and mitigation.

**Commitments to students**
All special education programs will continue to be staffed in alignment with state and county requirements, including certified teachers, paraprofessionals, and related service providers. Decisions are guided by each student's Individualized Education Program (IEP) and are mandated to comply with all legal and educational standards.
2026_000_specialeducation_board_narrativ.verbose:
Titled "Board Narrative Summary — Special Education Budget Reductions, Proposed Reduction Scenario" and dated June 2026, the paper explains to the Troy School District Board of Education how the proposed special education reductions were developed and how those specific reductions connect to the broader budget plan presented to the Board. It opens by stating that special education remains one of the district's highest priorities and one of its largest areas of investment.

SCORING METHOD AND TIER DEFINITIONS
The proposals were produced through the district's structured scoring process. Each was evaluated across six weighted criteria: impact on student learning, equity, legal and compliance risk, cost savings, feasibility, and stakeholder support. Weighted scores then determined tier placement. Tier 1 is defined as a strong candidate, scoring 4.0–5.0; Tier 2 as "consider," scoring 3.0–3.9; Tier 3 as high risk, requiring further study, scoring below 3.0. The summary states that savings figures reflect actual FTE and actual dollar savings as entered in the scoring matrix.

WHY SPECIAL EDUCATION IS PART OF THE CONVERSATION
The narrative attributes the inclusion of special education in the reduction scenario to six years of cost growth that is described as no longer sustainable within the district's structural budget. Between 2018–2019 and 2024–2025, special education costs rose 74% — an increase of more than $12.4 million — while the number of students served grew by only 3%. The accompanying comparison table reports Special Education Costs (IEP and non-IEP) of $16,744,610 in 2018–2019 and $29,210,999 in 2024–2025, a change of +$12,466,389 (74%); and Special Education Student Count of 1,332 in 2018–2019 and 1,367 in 2024–2025, a change of +35 (3%). The gap between cost growth and enrollment growth is identified as the central reason special education is included in the scenario.

A second driver is a state-led shift in how certain special education services are delivered. Several of the proposals align district staffing to new county-level service plans and county targets. Taken together, the reductions are described as intended to right-size staffing to current requirements while preserving the services students are entitled to.

COMMITMENTS TO STUDENTS
The summary states that the district's core obligations to students with disabilities do not change. All special education programs will continue to be staffed in alignment with state and county requirements, including certified teachers, paraprofessionals, and related service providers. Decisions are guided by each student's Individualized Education Program (IEP) and are mandated to comply with all legal and educational standards. As the district adapts to the state-led shift in service delivery, it will continue to provide services based on IEP needs and state requirements while making responsible adjustments to ensure the long-term sustainability of its programs.

SUMMARY OF PROPOSED REDUCTIONS
The proposed reductions fall into two categories, classroom instruction and non-instructional supports. Special Education – Classroom Instruction comprises 4 proposals with annual savings of $1,396,573 and a tier mix of 2 Tier 1 / 1 Tier 2 / 1 Tier 3. Special Education – Non-Instructional comprises 4 proposals with annual savings of $1,833,312 and a tier mix of 2 / 2 / 0. Total Special Education Reductions are stated as 8 proposals, $3,229,885 in annual savings, with a tier mix of 4 / 3 / 1.

CLASSROOM INSTRUCTION REDUCTIONS — $1,396,573
These proposals adjust instructional special education staffing to align with new county-level service plans and county staffing targets. Three of the four are described as strong or consider-level candidates; one — the adjustment of Teacher Consultant and Resource Room (TC/RR) staff to county targets — carries the highest risk in the special education set and is flagged for further Board discussion. The itemized proposals are:
• Adjust TC/RR staff to meet county targets (3.7 Elementary, 3.6 Secondary) — annual savings $635,100, weighted score 2.95, Tier 3, status "Flag for review."
• Teacher reduction based on new county level plan (3 L4, 1 ECP) — annual savings $348,000, score 4.10, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
• Paraprofessional reduction based on new county level plan — annual savings $236,270, score 4.10, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
• Elementary Resource Room paraprofessionals reduction — annual savings $177,203, score 3.85, Tier 2, status "Consider."
The subtotal for the category is $1,396,573. The narrative repeats that the TC/RR adjustment is the only Tier 3 proposal in the special education set, with a weighted score of 2.95, and that per the scoring framework it warrants further study before adoption.

NON-INSTRUCTIONAL REDUCTIONS — $1,833,312
These proposals reduce non-instructional support staffing. The largest single special education reduction in the entire scenario sits in this category: the reduction of general education Student Support Aides from 158 to 104 FTE, which the narrative says accounts for more than $1.3 million in savings. The remaining proposals adjust social worker, psychologist, and clerical staffing. The itemized proposals are:
• Student Support Aide – Gen Ed (from 158 to 104 FTE) — annual savings $1,334,362, score 4.15, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
• Social Workers reduction (from 24.4 to 21.4 FTE) — annual savings $348,000, score 3.90, Tier 2, status "Consider."
• Psychologist reduction (from 10 to 9 FTE) — annual savings $116,000, score 3.90, Tier 2, status "Consider."
• Special Education Secretary — annual savings $34,951, score 4.35, Tier 1, status "Recommended."
The subtotal for the category is $1,833,312. The narrative notes that the social worker and psychologist reductions are Tier 2 (consider) proposals and may benefit from phased implementation.

RISK AND PLANNING CONSIDERATIONS
Of the eight special education proposals, four are Tier 1 (recommended), three are Tier 2 (consider, with additional planning), and one is Tier 3 (high risk). In practical terms, the narrative states that the four Tier 1 proposals — totaling roughly $1.95 million — are strong candidates with low risk and high feasibility and are recommended for inclusion; that the three Tier 2 proposals — the Elementary Resource Room paraprofessional, social worker, and psychologist reductions — may be included with additional planning, communication, or phased implementation; and that the single Tier 3 proposal, the TC/RR staffing adjustment to county targets, is flagged for further Board conversation before it is adopted. It adds that proposals scoring below 4.0 may still be included if savings are critical to meeting the reduction goal, but that they require additional planning, communication, and mitigation efforts.

HOW THE REDUCTIONS FIT THE OVERALL PLAN
Because special education is governed by IEPs and by state and county requirements, the proposals were scored with particular attention to legal and compliance risk and to equity impact. The stated intent is to bring staffing back into alignment with current service requirements and the state-led delivery model — not to reduce services students are entitled to receive — while contributing meaningfully toward closing the structural budget gap.

2026_001_m061626bdmtg.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held Tuesday, June 16, 2026 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, called to order by President Anne at 7:18 p.m. and adjourned at 9:03 p.m. The session opened with a public hearing on the 2026/2027 proposed budget presented by Mr. Trudel, adopted resolutions supporting safe gun storage and urging the Governor and Legislature to pass the 2026/2027 School Aid Budget by July 1, and approved three purchases from the 2023 Capital Projects Fund, the largest being $2,464,089.00 in school buses awarded to Hoekstra Transportation.
2026_001_m061626bdmtg.page:
**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education, Regular Meeting Minutes, Tuesday, June 16, 2026, Service Center, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. Called to order by President Anne at 7:18 p.m.; adjourned at 9:03 p.m.

**Attendance**
Present: President Anne and Board members Alic, Melton, Potts, and Zendler. Absent: Mr. Haupt and Dr. Philippart. Also present: Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Moran, Anderson, Montante, Pagel, and Trudel. Approximately 50 members of the audience attended.

**Public hearing — 2026/2027 proposed budget**
Mr. Trudel presented an overview of the 2025-2026 final budget amendments and the 2026-2027 budget proposals, covering taxable values, the Headlee amendment, homestead millage comparisons, general fund versus ancillary funds, the capital project fund, common debt fund, sinking fund, capital maintenance fund, special revenue funds, food service fund, Troy Career Center fund, community service fund, Troy Preschool fund, and student activities fund.

**Resolutions adopted**

| Resolution | Moved / supported | Vote |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resolution In Support Of Gun Safety And Safe Gun Storage | Zendler / Alic | Yes 5, No 0, Absent Haupt and Philippart |
| Resolution urging the Governor and Legislature to pass the 2026/2027 School Aid Budget by July 1st | Alic / Zendler | Yes 5, No 0, Absent Haupt and Philippart |

The gun safety resolution directs the Superintendent to periodically communicate the importance of safe firearm storage during gun violence awareness month and to disseminate material annually in the district's annual notification materials, and commits the Board and Superintendent to continued work with local law enforcement, medical and mental health agencies, and non-profits. The School Aid resolution calls on the Legislature and Governor to act before July 1 and directs that copies be forwarded to the district's state House and Senate representatives and the Governor's office. Both were certified by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Board of Education, under the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976.

**Consent agenda (items A through J)**
Moved by Mrs. Alic, supported by Dr. Melton. Items: minutes of the May 19, 2026 Special Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report – April 2026; Food Service Contract Renewal; MHSAA Membership 2026/2027; 2025/2026 Budget Amendment; 2026/2027 Budget Appropriations Resolution; Common Debt Fund Resolution; OCSBA Association Bylaws Amendment; OCSBA new resolution opposing tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege; AP Precalculus Textbook Adoption. Vote: Yes 4 – Alic, Anne, Melton, Zendler; No 1 – Potts; Absent Haupt and Philippart.

**Business — purchases from the 2023 Capital Projects Fund**

| Item | Vendor / detail | Amount | Vote |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MacBook/iPad Purchases | Apple MacBooks and iPads | $2,420,430.00 | Yes 5, No 0 |
| Bus Purchase | Hoekstra Transportation | $2,464,089.00 | Yes 5, No 0 |
| Smith Printers | Applied Innovation | $733,985.55 | Yes 5, No 0 |

**Other proceedings**
Additions and deletions: none. Public communication on agenda items: five community members addressed the Board and no action was taken. Personnel, Curriculum, non-agenda public communication, and Other: none.

**Board comments**
Topics included encouraging the community to contact legislators about passing the budget on time; thanks to public commenters; congratulations to the Class of 2026; Men's Mental Health Awareness Month; appreciation for secretaries; Board members requesting a special meeting to discuss budget reductions further; counselor ratios and special education positions; the August 4th ballot countywide Enhancement Millage at $780 per student, just under $9,000,000 to Troy School District; the public education landscape; Father's Day; and Juneteenth.

**Next meeting**
Tuesday, July 21st at 9:30 a.m. in the Administration Building. Minutes submitted by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (MH/jh).
2026_001_m061626bdmtg.verbose:
Regular meeting minutes of the Troy Board of Education for Tuesday, June 16, 2026, held at the Troy School District Services Building (Service Center), 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:18 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, Board members Alic, Melton, Potts, and Zendler were present; Mr. Haupt and Dr. Philippart were absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Moran, Anderson, Montante, Pagel, and Trudel. Approximately 50 members of the audience attended. The meeting opened with the Pledge of Allegiance and adjourned at 9:03 p.m.

PUBLIC HEARING: 2026/2027 PROPOSED BUDGET
Mr. Trudel shared an overview of the 2025-2026 final budget amendments as well as the 2026-2027 budget proposals. His presentation addressed taxable values, the Headlee amendment, homestead millage comparisons, general fund versus ancillary funds, the capital project fund, the common debt fund, the sinking fund, the capital maintenance fund, special revenue funds, the food service fund, the Troy Career Center fund, the community service fund, the Troy Preschool fund, and the student activities fund.

RECOGNITION: RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF GUN SAFETY AND SAFE GUN STORAGE
Moved by Mrs. Zendler and supported by Mrs. Alic. The whereas clauses state that the safety and well-being of students, teachers, and staff is a top priority in the Troy School District; that firearms are now the leading cause of death among U.S. children and adolescents due to rising rates of homicide, suicide, and unintentional shootings, compounded by social inequities, increased access to guns, and insufficient safety measures; that rates of death from firearms among ages 14 to 17 are higher than motor vehicle-related death rates, and that middle and high school age children in the U.S. are now more likely to die as the result of a firearm injury than from any other single cause of death; that according to a report from the US Secret Service, in incidents of gun violence on school grounds 76% of attackers acquired a firearm from the home of a parent or another close relative; that since 2025 there have been over 240 unintentional shootings by children, resulting in 39 deaths and 72 injuries nationally; that more than 28,000 Americans are estimated to have died by suicide using firearms in 2025; that research indicates close to 5 million US children live in a home with a loaded and unlocked firearm; that evidence strongly suggests secure firearm storage is an essential component of any effective strategy to keep the community safe; that keeping students, teachers, and staff safe from the threat of gun violence should be the responsibility of all adult stakeholders within the school district; and that preventative measures require action now.

The resolved clauses direct the Superintendent to periodically communicate the importance of safe firearm storage and other firearm safety and violence prevention measures during gun violence awareness month, and to disseminate material on an annual basis stressing the importance of secure storage of firearms by including it in the district's annual notification materials; commit the Board and Superintendent to continue working with local law enforcement agencies, medical and mental health agencies, and non-profit organizations to inform district parents of their obligations regarding secure storage of firearms in their homes as well as other gun violence prevention safety measures; and state that the resolution shall not be construed to conflict with any existing Michigan or federal law. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Haupt and Philippart absent; the resolution was declared adopted. A certification by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Board of Education, attests that the resolution was duly adopted at a regular meeting held on the 16th day of June, 2026, conducted with public notice given in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, being Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976.

RESOLUTION URGING PASSAGE OF THE 2026/2027 SCHOOL AID BUDGET BY JULY 1ST
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Zendler. The whereas clauses note that with only two weeks remaining in the fiscal year for schools the Legislature had not yet passed a School Aid Budget; that last year the budget was not passed until after the Constitutional October 1 deadline, forcing districts to make critical staffing and programming decisions based on speculation rather than certainty, and that without a budget schools cannot responsibly plan for staffing, class sizes, transportation, or essential services; that Troy School District is legally obligated to complete its budget by the end of June and will fulfill that obligation, but without certainty from Lansing will again be forced to consider freezing programs, delaying hires, and laying off staff; that the framework for a responsible School Aid fund budget already exists within the three proposals under consideration; that focus should remain on passing a responsible, balanced budget rather than beginning discussions on major reforms, with significant property tax changes or other structural changes deserving thorough debate separate from the budget; and that policymakers must complete a School Aid budget including an inflationary increase to the foundation allowance, weighted funding for at-risk and ELL students, an end to the diversion of K12 dollars away from the classroom, and a fix to school safety and mental health funding. The resolved clauses call on the Legislature and the Governor to pass the School Aid Budget before July 1 and direct that a copy be forwarded to the district's representatives in the Michigan House of Representatives and the Michigan Senate as well as the Governor's office. The vote was Yes 5, No 0, with Haupt and Philippart absent; the motion was declared adopted, certified by Matt Haupt, Secretary.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS / PUBLIC COMMUNICATION
Additions and deletions: none. During public communication on agenda items, five community members addressed the Board; no action was taken. Public communication on non-agenda items: none. Personnel: none. Curriculum: none. Other: none.

GENERAL – CONSENT AGENDA
Moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Melton that the Board approve items A through J on the consent agenda: minutes of the May 19, 2026 Special Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report – April 2026; Food Service Contract Renewal; Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) Membership – 2026/2027; 2025/2026 Budget Amendment; 2026/2027 Budget Appropriations Resolution; Common Debt Fund Resolution; approval of OCSBA Association Bylaws Amendment; approval of an OCSBA new resolution opposing tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege; and AP Precalculus Textbook Adoption. The vote was Yes 4 – Alic, Anne, Melton, Zendler; No 1 – Potts; Absent Haupt and Philippart.

BUSINESS ITEMS
MacBook/iPad Purchases: moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mrs. Alic that the district purchase Apple MacBooks and iPads in the amount of $2,420,430.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote Yes 5, No 0, Absent Haupt and Philippart.
Bus Purchase: moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Dr. Melton that the bid for school buses be awarded to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $2,464,089.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote Yes 5, No 0, Absent Haupt and Philippart.
Smith Printers: moved by Mrs. Potts and supported by Mrs. Zendler that the purchase of printers be awarded to Applied Innovation in the amount of $733,985.55, approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Vote Yes 5, No 0, Absent Haupt and Philippart.

BOARD COMMENTS
Listed comments included encouraging the community to reach out to legislators to pass the budget on time; thanks to speakers who spoke during public comment, with the note that the board hears them; congratulations to the Class of 2026 graduates; Men's Mental Health Awareness Month; appreciation for secretaries; Board members requesting a special meeting to discuss budget reductions further; counselor ratios and special education positions; the August 4th ballot countywide millage, under which $780 per student would come from the Enhancement Millage, just under $9,000,000 to Troy School District; a comment that the public education landscape is not good; and Happy Father's Day and Juneteenth celebration.

ADJOURNMENT AND NEXT MEETING
The next Board meeting was announced for Tuesday, July 21st at 9:30 a.m. in the Administration Building. The meeting was adjourned at 9:03 p.m. Minutes respectfully submitted by Matt Haupt, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the notation MH/jh.

2026_002_coop_letter_mhsaa_executive_boa.paragraph: A letter dated June 15, 2026 from Matt Jansen, Troy School District Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment, asks the MHSAA Executive Board to waive the cooperative team enrollment limitation so Troy High School and Troy Athens High School may form a combined "Troy United" boys lacrosse program beginning in 2026-27. The two schools' combined enrollment of 3,936 students exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements. The request is framed by a projected $12.1 million district budget deficit and by declining participation, with only 41 players projected to return across the two programs before incoming freshmen.
2026_002_coop_letter_mhsaa_executive_boa.page:
**Document**
Letter dated June 15, 2026 to the Members of the MHSAA Executive Board, on Troy School District District Athletics letterhead — Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., Superintendent of Schools; Matt Jansen, Director, Athletics; 1522 E. Big Beaver Rd., Troy, Michigan 48083; 248.823.5154, fax 248.823.5133. Signed by Matt Jansen, Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment.

**Request**
Approval of a waiver to the current cooperative team enrollment limitation to allow Troy High School and Troy Athens High School to form a cooperative boys lacrosse program beginning with the 2026-27 school year, operating as a single "Troy United" program.

**Enrollment**

| School | Enrollment |
| --- | --- |
| Troy High School | 2,127 |
| Troy Athens High School | 1,809 |
| Combined | 3,936 |

The combined figure exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements, which is why a waiver is sought.

**Financial context**
The district is facing a projected $12.1 million budget deficit entering the 2026-27 school year. As part of district-wide reductions, the Athletics Department has been tasked with reducing expenditures by approximately $100,000. The district recently discontinued financial support for non-MHSAA sanctioned sports, including synchronized swimming and boys and girls water polo; those programs moved to self-funded club status, generating approximately $50,000 in annual savings. A cooperative boys lacrosse program would provide an estimated annual savings of approximately $25,000.

**Participation**

| Measure | Troy High School | Troy Athens High School |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026 season participants | 48 | 31 |
| Graduating seniors | 21 | 13 |
| Projected returning participants | 26 | 15 |

Combined returning participation is stated as 41 players before the addition of incoming freshmen. Of the 15 projected returners at Athens, only one participated at the varsity level during the 2026 season; the remaining 14 had never played lacrosse prior to 2026. Athens attempted to field both varsity and junior varsity teams but could not consistently maintain enough healthy student-athletes to sustain junior varsity competition through the season.

**Program stability**
Following the 2026 season, the Troy Athens varsity boys lacrosse coach informed the district of his decision to step down, citing as a significant factor the ongoing difficulty of building and sustaining a program with limited participation. Troy Athens has historically participated in a cooperative arrangement with Avondale Schools, which in recent years has yielded no more than two players annually and contributed no participants during the 2026 season; the letter concludes that partnership is no longer viable.

**Precedent cited**
Within the Oakland Activities Association and surrounding communities: Farmington and North Farmington; Royal Oak and Berkley; Birmingham Groves and Birmingham Seaholm; Waterford Mott and Waterford Kettering; Milford and Lakeland; the Livonia Public Schools combined program; South Lyon's combined program; Bishop Foley and Clawson; Brandon and Holly; the St. Clair Shores cooperative program; and Eisenhower and Utica.

**Position**
The letter states the request is not intended to create a competitive advantage but to preserve participation opportunities, maintain both varsity and junior varsity levels of competition, and sustain access to boys lacrosse. It notes the proposal has the full support and approval of Troy School District administration, including the Superintendent, Assistant Superintendent, both high school principals, and the Athletic Department.
2026_002_coop_letter_mhsaa_executive_boa.verbose:
Correspondence dated June 15, 2026, addressed to the Members of the MHSAA Executive Board, sent on Troy School District District Athletics letterhead listing Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., Superintendent of Schools, and Matt Jansen, Director, Athletics, at 1522 E. Big Beaver Rd., Troy, Michigan 48083, telephone 248.823.5154, fax 248.823.5133. The letter is signed by Matt Jansen, Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment, and carries the footer "An Equal Opportunity/Affirmative Action Employer."

THE REQUEST
On behalf of the Troy School District, the letter requests approval of a waiver to the current cooperative team enrollment limitation to allow Troy High School and Troy Athens High School to form a cooperative boys lacrosse program beginning with the 2026-27 school year. The combined enrollment of the two high schools is 3,936 students, with Troy High School enrolling 2,127 students and Troy Athens High School enrolling 1,809 students. The letter acknowledges that this total exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements but argues that the circumstances warrant special consideration and approval.

FINANCIAL CONTEXT
The Troy School District is described as currently facing a projected $12.1 million budget deficit entering the 2026-27 school year. As part of district-wide reductions, the Athletics Department has been tasked with reducing expenditures by approximately $100,000. To address these financial challenges, the district recently discontinued financial support for non-MHSAA sanctioned sports, including synchronized swimming and boys and girls water polo. Those programs have transitioned to self-funded club status, generating approximately $50,000 in annual savings. The letter calls this a difficult decision and states that additional measures are necessary to maintain sustainable athletic opportunities for students. A cooperative boys lacrosse program between Troy High School and Troy Athens High School would provide an estimated annual savings of approximately $25,000 while preserving participation opportunities for student-athletes at both schools.

PARTICIPATION AND PROGRAM SUSTAINABILITY
The letter emphasizes that the request is driven more by participation numbers and program sustainability than solely by financial considerations. During the 2026 boys lacrosse season, Troy High School had 48 participants while Troy Athens High School had 31 participants. Troy High School is graduating 21 seniors and Troy Athens High School is graduating 13 seniors. This leaves projected returning participation numbers of only 26 student-athletes at Troy High School and 15 student-athletes at Troy Athens High School, for a combined total of 41 returning players before the addition of incoming freshmen.

The situation at Troy Athens is described as particularly concerning. Of the 15 projected returning players, only one participated at the varsity level during the 2026 season; the remaining 14 players had never played lacrosse prior to the 2026 season. Although Athens attempted to field both varsity and junior varsity teams in the spring, the program was unable to consistently maintain enough healthy student-athletes to sustain junior varsity competition throughout the season.

COACHING AND PRIOR COOPERATIVE ARRANGEMENT
These challenges are said to have affected program leadership and long-term stability. Following the 2026 season, the Troy Athens varsity boys lacrosse coach informed the district of his decision to step down, with a significant factor being the ongoing difficulty of building and sustaining a program with limited participation numbers. The letter presents this as further illustration of the challenges facing the Athens program and the need for a more sustainable model. Historically, Troy Athens has participated in a cooperative arrangement with Avondale Schools, but that partnership has not provided the participation numbers necessary to sustain the program: in recent years the cooperative agreement has yielded no more than two players annually, and during the 2026 season Avondale contributed no participants. The letter concludes that the Avondale partnership is no longer a viable long-term solution.

RATIONALE FOR A COMBINED PROGRAM
The letter states that one of the fundamental goals of interscholastic athletics is to provide meaningful participation and developmental opportunities for as many student-athletes as possible. A cooperative program would allow the district to maintain both varsity and junior varsity competition, ensuring that beginning and developing players have an appropriate environment in which to learn, improve, and remain engaged in the sport; without sufficient numbers to sustain a junior varsity program, opportunities for skill development and long-term participation are significantly diminished. Establishing a single "Troy United" boys lacrosse program is presented as a stable structure that supports program numbers while preserving access and opportunity for student-athletes from both schools, aligning with the educational mission of the MHSAA by prioritizing participation, student development, and the long-term viability of boys lacrosse within the community.

REGIONAL PRECEDENT
The letter argues the request is consistent with cooperative programs that already exist throughout the region. Within the Oakland Activities Association and surrounding communities, numerous school districts have been permitted to combine programs to preserve participation opportunities. Examples cited include Farmington and North Farmington, Royal Oak and Berkley, Birmingham Groves and Birmingham Seaholm, and Waterford Mott and Waterford Kettering. Additional area examples cited are Milford and Lakeland, the Livonia Public Schools combined program, South Lyon's combined program, Bishop Foley and Clawson, Brandon and Holly, the St. Clair Shores cooperative program, and Eisenhower and Utica. The Troy School District states it is simply seeking the same opportunity to preserve a viable boys lacrosse program for its students.

CLOSING POSITION AND APPROVALS
Approval of the waiver would allow the district to establish a single "Troy United" boys lacrosse program representing both Troy High School and Troy Athens High School, providing the participation numbers necessary to maintain both varsity and junior varsity opportunities while supporting the district's ongoing financial sustainability efforts. The letter states the request is not intended to create a competitive advantage but rather to preserve participation opportunities, maintain both levels of competition, and ensure that student-athletes in the Troy School District continue to have access to boys lacrosse in a sustainable and educationally sound manner. The proposal is reported to have already received the full support and approval of the Troy School District administration, including the Superintendent, the Assistant Superintendent, both high school principals, and the Athletic Department. The letter closes by respectfully requesting that the Executive Board grant the waiver to the cooperative enrollment limitation and approve the cooperative boys lacrosse program, thanking the board for its consideration and offering to provide any additional information the Council may require.
